frase_gancho.texto: Two figures face to face: the mark of Teotihuacán in Oaxaca.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the contacts between cities, we move on to the gods who watched over the fields. Look for a gray clay urn with thick goggle-like eye rings and fangs: it is Cocijo, the Zapotec god of rain.

guion_corto.texto: This small travertine slab, almost fifty centimeters tall, blends two worlds. It was found at Monte Albán and dates to between the years three hundred fifty and four hundred of our era. On it, two figures stand face to face, and between them and along the edges there are glyphs from different traditions. One is dressed in the manner of the Central Highlands, the other in the Zapotec manner. Specialists consider it one of the clearest traces that Monte Albán and great Teotihuacán had direct contact, and it has been interpreted as the memory of an official visit between the two cities. It is a meeting of powers, told on a small stone.

guion_largo.texto:
Sometimes a small stone tells an enormous story. This slab is small, almost half a meter tall, but it speaks of the relationship between two of the most powerful cities of their time: Teotihuacán, in the Valley of Mexico, and Monte Albán, in Oaxaca. When it was made, around the year three hundred fifty, Teotihuacán already had centuries of greatness behind it, and its influence reached far. Monte Albán was another capital, with its own style, its own writing and its own way of seeing the world.

That relationship was no legend. In Teotihuacán itself there was a neighborhood where people from Oaxaca lived, called Tlailotlacan in Nahuatl, with tombs and pottery in the Zapotec style. Archaeologists know it well, because objects from Oaxaca were found there mixed with those of the Central Highlands. They were probably merchants, artisans or ambassadors, who stayed for years or for generations. And the exchange went in both directions: at Monte Albán, blades of the greenish obsidian from Pachuca have been found, a material that Teotihuacán controlled, the same obsidian you already saw turned into blades in the Teotihuacán Hall. Teotihuacán had a Zapotec neighborhood; and Monte Albán, it seems, remembered the relationship in stone.

Look at the scene. Two figures confront each other. One wears clothing and a headdress that recall the style of the Central Highlands; the other, the Zapotec style. Between them and along the edges there are glyphs, and signs from two different traditions can be recognized. It is rare to see a dialogue like this on a single slab, with two cultures represented as equals, without one crushing the other.

What does it say exactly? That is where the debate lies. The most repeated reading speaks of an official visit, perhaps an embassy sealing a commercial or political agreement. Other specialists prefer to speak only of contacts and of an exchange of objects and ideas. The word “treaty” is an interpretation, not something the stone says clearly. What is certain is that two worlds looked each other in the face, and that in Monte Albán someone decided this meeting deserved to be carved. That matters for another reason: very few long texts from Teotihuacán survive, so pieces like this one, where Zapotec writing sits alongside signs from the Central Highlands, are among the few windows we have for hearing how the two cities spoke to each other.

It is also interesting to see who does not appear. There is no conqueror and no conquered. It seems that Monte Albán was never subdued by Teotihuacán; it kept its style and its independence, and its relationship with the great city was closer to diplomacy than to war. If you compare it with [the Dancers](mna_s07_danzante_montealban), which you have just seen, it is a very different way of telling the story of power.

And think about the distance. Between the two cities lie more than three hundred kilometers of mountains, with no horses and no wheels. Those who carried messages, jade, feathers, shell and news went on foot, loaded on their backs. Mesoamerica was an immense network, stitched together by roads and by the people who traveled them.

That is why, when you see similar gods in faraway places, the explanation is usually not chance. The gods traveled, just like ideas. Sometimes the name, the face or the myth changes, but the need is the same, like the rain. And that is precisely the theme of the next piece.

texto.Period: Early Classic (Monte Albán IIIA, around 350-400 AD)
texto.Material: Travertine / Mexican onyx, engraved and inlaid
texto.Origin: Mound X, Great Plaza of Monte Albán, Oaxaca
texto.Dimensions: 49 cm high x 30 cm wide x 7 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Mesoamerican peoples lived isolated from one another.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were connected by trade and diplomatic routes: porters on foot carried jade, feathers, shell and news hundreds of kilometers.
